newsitem.title: GERMANY: Airlines like the look of German mobile phone ban.
newsitem.headline: Airlines like the look of German mobile phone ban.

text.p: A tough new draft law in Germany setting a maximum two-year jail sentence for people who use mobile phones and other electronic devices on board aircraft was broadly welcomed by the airline industry on Friday.
The bill covers laptop computers, video cameras and any equipment that might affect an aircraft's electronics and communications systems.

If approved by parliament, it could come into effect by the middle of next year and be applied to any flight which even partially uses Germany's busy airspace, Bonn's Transport Ministry said earlier this week.
Most airlines across the world discourage passengers on safety grounds from using mobile telephones, but it is virtually unknown for countries to give these restrictions the force of law.

"The details of the draft are with our legal department at the moment. But certainly we welcome the part of the law relating to radio-based equipment," said a spokesman for German airline Deutsche Lufthansa AG.
There is, however, little concrete evidence that mobile phones or other gadgets can directly disrupt aircraft systems.

"There have been no incidents that can be directly linked to such devices. There have only been cases where we would not like to rule out the possible interference of radio-based equipment," the Lufthansa spokesman conceded.

The Brussels-based Association of European Airlines (AEA) said there had only been instances where such devices "appeared to lead to irregularities" in an aircraft's function. But it still expected airlines broadly to back the move.

"This is probably one law where we won't be coming out and saying: 'This is over-regulation,'" AEA spokesman David Henderson said. "Airlines will probably be glad to be able to point their passengers to such a ruling."

Henderson said Europe's Joint Aviation Authority (JAA) had already formulated the wording of an onboard ban on portable electronic devices but noted it was "up to the countries themselves if they...decide to put some meat on it".
It remains unclear what kind of jurisdiction Bonn will seek for the law.
A Transport Ministry spokesman said on Friday it was envisaged the ban would apply for the duration of any flight using German airspace, even if much of the route was over another country.

But it remains questionable whether offenders outside German airspace will be handed back for prosecution under German laws, or whether the other country involved would insist its own legal framework should apply.

The ban comes as a number of airlines have started installing onboard telephones for use by passengers, prompting some observers to suggest that the industry's support for tighter laws has a degree of economic self-interest.

Air France, which this week announced it was launching a "Jetphone" service for passengers on all short- and medium-distance flights, said the margins available from such services were not a key factor.

"This is more just a service we think customers will want. The installation of such systems requires a considerable outlay and much of the fee charged goes to the telecom provider," said a spokeswoman for Air France in Frankfurt.
Research conducted last year showed that a third of European passengers wanted to be able to make inflight calls, most of them for business reasons. -- Frankfurt Newsroom +49 69 756525
